DISTRIBUTIVE JUSTICE Who gets the benefits? Who bears the burdens? Focuses on the distribution of green space, clean air and shade (goods) vs noise, flooding and displacement (burdens) across social groups. Classic inequity: wealthier, whiter neighbourhoods have more and better-quality green space. Source: Schlosberg (2007) Ch.2; Rigolon (2016); Wolch et al. (2014) — PROCEDURAL JUSTICE Was the decision-making process fair and inclusive? Concerns the fairness of the process — not just the outcomes. A process can produce good outcomes yet still be procedurally unjust if certain groups were excluded or had no real influence. NOTE: high IAP2 level ≠ procedural justice if participants were unrepresentative. Source: Schlosberg (2007) Ch.3; Fung (2006); IAP2 (2018) — RECOGNITIONAL JUSTICE Whose knowledge, identities and cultures are acknowledged? Asks whether the intervention respects the identities, knowledge systems, cultures and histories of all groups — especially historically marginalised ones. Example of misrecognition: a park that erases an informal gathering space used by an immigrant community. Source: Schlosberg (2007) Ch.4; Fraser (2000); Fricker (2007)
Options: Procedural, Distributive, Recognitional or not evoked
